sections.heading: Selling AI by the seat
bullets: Enterprise software's classic unit is the seat: a fixed monthly price per employee — predictable for buyers, recurring for sellers — and AI assistants are sold the same way, priced as an add-on seat atop an existing productivity suite

The economics hinge on a mismatch: revenue is flat per seat but cost is per-query inference — a heavy user can consume their subscription price in compute — so margins depend on usage distributions and relentless per-token cost reduction

Distribution beats model quality in the enterprise: a good-enough assistant already inside the tools, security review, and billing relationship of hundreds of millions of workers wins deployments a better standalone model never gets to bid on

Watch the metric shift as the market matures: seats sold measures sales-force success; seats actively used measures whether the product earns renewal — enterprise AI's open question is converting licenses into daily habits

sections.heading: Funding a lab with a cloud: the compute-for-equity structure
bullets: The structure: a cloud provider invests billions in a frontier AI lab, much of which effectively returns as the lab's spending on that provider's compute — the lab gets scarce capacity plus capital; the provider gets equity upside plus an anchor tenant

Accounting makes the loop visible: under the equity method — how investors account for large minority stakes — the backer books its ownership share of the lab's profit or loss each quarter, so a private lab's burn rate surfaces in its investor's public filings

The circularity critique: the same dollars can count as the provider's cloud revenue and the lab's funding, so reported demand partly reflects the investor's own money round-tripping — real capacity gets built, but the growth signal deserves discounting

Mature versions convert dependency into contract: exclusivity gives way to committed multi-year purchase agreements, defined intellectual-property rights, and independent verification clauses — terms both sides can plan, and diversify, around

sections.heading: Buying power that doesn't exist yet
bullets: A nuclear restart revives a shut-down reactor: the machine, grid connection, and licensed site already exist, so cost and schedule beat new construction by years — the scarce inputs are regulatory re-approval, trained staff, and fuel, not concrete

The offtake makes it happen: a 20-year commitment to buy the plant's full output at a fixed price hands the owner bankable revenue — the buyer's balance sheet effectively finances the restart, a role governments historically played

A fusion power purchase agreement extends the logic to the unbuilt: committing to buy from a first-of-a-kind fusion plant is partly an option contract — modest cost if the technology slips, first-customer position and priced power if it arrives

The portfolio view is a maturity ladder: restarts can deliver firm carbon-free power this decade, new fission next decade, fusion after — laddering offtakes across horizons buys near-term certainty and long-term optionality with the same instrument

sections.heading: Reliability as software: regions, zones, and the vanishing UPS
bullets: Cloud reliability is architected in layers: a region is a metro-area cluster of data centers; availability zones are independent failure domains inside it — separate power, cooling, and networking, but close enough to mirror data between them in real time

The philosophy shift: rather than making every building unkillable with uninterruptible power supplies (UPS — battery bridges) and diesel generators, replicate the workload across zones and let software route around any single failure

Availability is priced in 'nines': 99.9% allows about nine hours of downtime a year, 99.99% under one hour — each extra nine multiplies cost, so the design question is which workloads need hardware-level protection versus software-level redundancy

Carried to its conclusion, a data center can drop backup power entirely: accept a slightly lower availability target for that one building, buy firm power upstream from the grid, and bank the capital — a bet that reliability lives in the fleet, not the facility

sections.heading: Shipping AI safely: gates as engineering
bullets: Frontier AI deployment runs through staged gates: internal evaluations (standardized tests probing capabilities and failure modes), red-teaming, limited previews, then general release — a pipeline with go/no-go criteria, not a judgment call at the end

Red-teaming imports a security-industry discipline: paid adversaries who think like misusers hunt the jailbreaks, prompt injections, and harmful-output paths before the public finds them — and their findings gate progression to the next stage

In the enterprise, safety is a purchasable feature: content filtering, audit logs, data-residency guarantees, and indemnification are what allow regulated industries — banks, hospitals, governments — to deploy at all; compliance work converts directly into addressable market

The gates manage a two-sided risk: ship too fast and incidents destroy enterprise trust; gate too hard and customers adopt a rival's model — deployment policy is a product decision made under competitive pressure, not a purely technical one

sections.heading: The moat that pays for the machines
bullets: Switching costs are the old moat funding the new buildout: an organization's documents, workflows, permissions, and training live inside a productivity ecosystem — migrating is a multi-year project few ever attempt, which makes the revenue annuity-like

Bundling converts the moat into distribution: adding an AI assistant to a suite the customer already licenses makes the marginal sale an upsell conversation instead of a competitive bake-off — the cheapest customer acquisition in software

Multi-year enterprise agreements aggregate it into visibility: contracts spanning operating systems, productivity, cloud, and security lock in cash flow measurable years ahead — infrastructure spending that is substantially pre-sold before ground breaks

The strategic consequence: a company whose capex is underwritten by contracted enterprise demand can outspend rivals financed by equity-market hope — the boring moat, not the frontier model, is what actually pays for the machines

flashcards.q: What's the core margin risk in per-seat pricing for AI assistants?
flashcards.a: Revenue is fixed per seat but cost is per-query inference — a power user can burn their whole subscription price in compute. Margins survive only if usage stays distributed and the per-token cost of serving answers keeps falling faster than usage grows.

flashcards.q: Why does distribution often beat model quality in enterprise AI?
flashcards.a: A good-enough assistant already inside the customer's tools, security review, and billing relationship wins deployments a better standalone model never gets to bid on. Enterprise purchases are decided by procurement friction and trust as much as capability.

flashcards.q: Why does 'seats actively used' matter more than 'seats sold'?
flashcards.a: Seats sold measures the sales force; seats used measures whether the product became a habit that survives renewal negotiations. A license that nobody opens is future churn already booked — the gap between the two numbers is the honest health metric of enterprise AI.

flashcards.q: How does a compute-for-equity partnership work?
flashcards.a: A cloud provider invests billions in an AI lab, and much of the money returns as the lab's spending on that provider's compute. The lab gets scarce capacity and capital; the provider gets equity upside and an anchor tenant. The same dollars appear as both funding and revenue — which is also the critique.

flashcards.q: How can a private lab's losses show up in a public company's filings?
flashcards.a: Under the equity method of accounting, an investor holding a large minority stake books its ownership share of the investee's profit or loss every quarter. The backer's income statement therefore leaks a signal about the private lab's burn rate that the lab itself never publishes.

flashcards.q: Why is restarting a shut-down nuclear plant so much cheaper than building new?
flashcards.a: The reactor, grid connection, and licensed site already exist — the billion-dollar, decade-long parts are done. What remains is regulatory re-approval, rebuilding a trained workforce, refurbishment, and fuel. That's why a restart can deliver firm carbon-free power years before any new plant could.

flashcards.q: How does a long-term offtake finance a power plant?
flashcards.a: A creditworthy buyer committing to purchase decades of output at agreed prices gives the plant owner bankable revenue — lenders finance the project against that contract. The buyer's balance sheet substitutes for the government support such projects historically needed.

flashcards.q: What is the logic of signing a PPA with a fusion plant that doesn't exist?
flashcards.a: It's partly an option contract: modest downside if the technology slips, but first-customer position, negotiated pricing, and early insight if it arrives. The signature itself also helps the developer raise capital — a purchase commitment from a credible buyer is evidence the market is real.

An independent failure domain within a cloud region — its own power, cooling, and networking — close enough to other zones for real-time data mirroring. Workloads replicated across zones survive a whole-building failure because software reroutes around it.

flashcards.q: How do 'nines' of availability relate to cost?
flashcards.a: 99.9% availability allows about nine hours of downtime a year; 99.99% allows under one. Each added nine roughly multiplies the redundancy cost. The design question is which workloads truly need hardware-level protection and which can accept software-level redundancy at far lower cost.

flashcards.q: Why would a data center be designed with no backup generators or UPS at all?
flashcards.a: If workloads are replicated across independent zones, a single building can accept a lower availability target — so you buy firm grid power upstream, skip the batteries and diesels, and save the capital. Resilience is relocated from the facility to the fleet's software.

flashcards.q: What is red-teaming in AI deployment?
flashcards.a: Paid adversaries systematically attack a model before release — hunting jailbreaks, prompt injections, and harmful-output paths the way security researchers attack software. Findings feed mitigations and gate progression through staged rollout. In enterprise AI, this discipline is also a sales requirement: regulated customers buy the gates as much as the model.
